title: Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat

toc.title: 9.1 Linear, superficial and cubical expansion and their relation
9.2 Real and apparent expansion of liquids
9.3 Heat capacity, specific heat capacity and the method of mixtures
9.4 Latent heat of fusion and vaporization; the triple point

html:
Heat and Thermodynamics carries 7 of the 50 Physics questions (official MEC weightage), with about 2 questions from this chapter.

The marks here are almost all numerical or definitional: a coefficient of expansion and its relation to the other two, a liquid that overflows a vessel, a mixture that settles at a final temperature, an ice–water–steam sum, or a clock that loses seconds on a hot day.

Every one of them is a one-line formula provided the phase bookkeeping is done in the right order. That order is what this chapter teaches.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • \Delta L = L\alpha\Delta T, \Delta A = A\beta\Delta T, \Delta V = V\gamma\Delta T, with \beta = 2\alpha and \gamma = 3\alpha.
  • A hole in a heated plate grows; a clamped rod develops stress Y\alpha\Delta T; a pendulum clock loses time \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta\theta per unit time.
  • Real and apparent expansion: \gamma_r = \gamma_a + \gamma_v (real = apparent + vessel); the level in a vessel first dips, then rises.
  • Q = mc\Delta T, Q = C\Delta T, and the method of mixtures m_1c_1(\theta_1-\theta) = (m_2c_2 + Wc_w)(\theta-\theta_2).
  • Water equivalent W = m_c c_c / c_w; ignoring it makes the answer wrong in a predictable direction.
  • Q = mL; L_f = 3.36\times10^5\ \text{J kg}^{-1}, L_v = 2.26\times10^6\ \text{J kg}^{-1}; temperature stays constant during a phase change.
  • Newton's law of cooling: rate of loss of heat \propto excess temperature, so cooling is exponential.
  • The triple point of water: 273.16 K at 611 Pa, the only state where ice, water and vapour coexist.

9.1 Linear, superficial and cubical expansion and their relation

Almost every substance expands when heated at constant pressure.

The atoms vibrate about fixed mean positions; the vibration is not symmetric about the mean position — the repulsive side of the potential is steeper than the attractive side — so the average separation grows as the amplitude grows.

Nothing in the solid is pushed apart by a "force of heat"; the spacing simply increases.

The three coefficients

Coefficients of expansion

For a rise in temperature \Delta T:

  • Linear: \alpha = \dfrac{1}{L}\dfrac{\Delta L}{\Delta T} — fractional increase in length per kelvin.
  • Superficial: \beta = \dfrac{1}{A}\dfrac{\Delta A}{\Delta T} — fractional increase in area per kelvin.
  • Cubical (volume): \gamma = \dfrac{1}{V}\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta T} — fractional increase in volume per kelvin.

All three have SI unit K⁻¹ (numerically the same as °C⁻¹, because a temperature difference is the same on both scales). They are properties of the material, not of the size or shape of the body: a long rod and a short rod of copper have the same α.

Quantity Symbol Formula Unit
Change in length \Delta L L\alpha\Delta T m
Change in area \Delta A A\beta\Delta T m²
Change in volume \Delta V V\gamma\Delta T m³
New length L' L(1+\alpha\Delta T) m

Typical values at room temperature (K⁻¹):

Material \alpha Material \alpha
Quartz (fused) 0.4\times10^{-6} Copper 1.7\times10^{-5}
Invar 1.2\times10^{-6} Brass 1.9\times10^{-5}
Glass 8\times10^{-6} Aluminium 2.4\times10^{-5}
Steel, iron 1.2\times10^{-5} Lead 2.9\times10^{-5}

Two things to read off this table. Invar was invented for pendulum rods and tape measures precisely because its α is ten times smaller than steel's.

And liquids and gases expand far more than solids: for mercury \gamma = 1.8\times10^{-4} K⁻¹, for water about 2.1\times10^{-4} K⁻¹, for air at constant pressure \gamma = 1/273 \approx 3.7\times10^{-3} K⁻¹.

A gas is some twenty times more expansive than a liquid and a few hundred times more than a solid.

Why β = 2α and γ = 3α

β = 2α and γ = 3α

Starting point. A cube of side L is heated through \Delta T; every side grows by the same fraction \alpha\Delta T. We want the coefficients of area and volume.

Setting up. L' = L(1+\alpha\Delta T), area A = L^2, volume V = L^3.

Step 1 — square the new side. A' = L'^2 = L^2(1+\alpha\Delta T)^2 = A(1 + 2\alpha\Delta T + \alpha^2\Delta T^2).

Step 2 — throw away the squared term. For a metal, \alpha\Delta T is about 10^{-5}\times50 = 5\times10^{-4}; its square is 2.5\times10^{-7}, a thousandth of the linear term.

Keeping only the first power, A' = A(1 + 2\alpha\Delta T), so \Delta A = A(2\alpha)\Delta T.

Step 3 — compare with the definition. \Delta A = A\beta\Delta T, hence \beta = 2\alpha.

Step 4 — cube the new side. V' = L'^3 = V(1+\alpha\Delta T)^3 = V(1 + 3\alpha\Delta T + 3\alpha^2\Delta T^2 + \alpha^3\Delta T^3), and again only the first power survives: \Delta V = V(3\alpha)\Delta T, hence \gamma = 3\alpha.

Result. \beta = 2\alpha and \gamma = 3\alpha.

What it means. The three coefficients are not independent: measure one and you have all three. The conditions are that the solid is isotropic (the same α in every direction — true for a metal, false for wood or a crystal) and that \alpha\Delta T \ll 1.

The classic wrong pair

Area uses 2\alpha, volume uses 3\alpha. Students who write \gamma = 3\alpha for an area, or \beta = \frac{3}{2}\alpha, lose the mark every time. Fix the picture in your head: length is one dimension, area two, volume three.

The relation holds for any linear dimension of the body, including a hole.

A plate with a circular hole is, geometrically, the same as a plate with a disc of the same material filling the hole — so on heating the disc grows and the hole grows with it. The hole does not close up.

This single fact is asked in some form in almost every paper.

Bimetallic strip

Two different metals — usually brass and iron — are riveted or welded along their whole length. Brass has the larger α (about 1.9\times10^{-5} against 1.2\times10^{-5} K⁻¹).

On heating, the brass side becomes longer than the iron side, so the strip can only stay joined by bending into an arc in which the brass is on the outside (the longer path).

On cooling the brass contracts more, so it ends up on the inside. The strip therefore bends towards the metal with the smaller α when heated.

Uses: the thermostat in an electric iron, a geyser or a refrigerator (the strip curls, breaks a contact, the heater switches off, and it straightens again when the temperature falls); the bimetallic thermometer; and temperature compensation in watches.

Thermal stress

If a rod is clamped at both ends, it cannot expand, and the "lost" expansion appears as an elastic strain:

\text{strain} = \frac{\Delta L}{L} = \alpha\Delta T, \qquad \sigma = Y\,\alpha\Delta T, \qquad F = YA\,\alpha\Delta T

where Y is Young's modulus. The stress is compressive on heating (the rod would have grown, so it is squeezed) and tensile on cooling.

This is why concrete roads are laid in slabs with tar-filled gaps, why railway rails are welded with expansion joints, and why a glass tumbler cracks when boiling water is poured into it: the inner surface tries to expand against a cold, unyielding outer surface.

Worked example 9.1 — the gap in a rail

Problem. Steel rails 20 m long are laid at 15 °C. What gap must be left between consecutive rails so that they just touch at 55 °C? (\alpha = 1.2\times10^{-5} K⁻¹.)

Solution. \Delta T = 40 K, so \Delta L = L\alpha\Delta T = 20\times1.2\times10^{-5}\times40 = 9.6\times10^{-3} m = 9.6 mm.

So a gap of about 1 cm — the growth of one rail — is left at each joint, which is why a train crossing a joint sets up the familiar clickety-click.

Worked example 9.2 — a clock on a hot day

Problem. A pendulum clock keeps correct time at 20 °C. Its rod is steel (\alpha = 2\times10^{-5} K⁻¹). How much time does it lose in one day at 35 °C?

Solution. The period is T_p = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}, so \frac{\Delta T_p}{T_p} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta L}{L} = \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta\theta.

With \Delta\theta = 15 K, the fractional change is \frac{1}{2}(2\times10^{-5})(15) = 1.5\times10^{-4}. In a day the clock runs slow by 1.5\times10^{-4}\times86400 = 12.96 s ≈ 13 s.

The pendulum is longer, so each swing takes longer, so the clock loses time. A cooling rod would make it gain.

Two one-line checks

For a heated body, ask "does the fractional change look like 10^{-4}?" — \alpha\Delta T for a metal and a 50 K rise is about 6\times10^{-4}, i.e. 0.06 %.

If your answer is a few per cent, you have used the wrong coefficient or the wrong power of ten. For a clock, remember the factor \frac{1}{2}: the period depends on \sqrt{L}, not on L.

9.2 Real and apparent expansion of liquids

A liquid has no fixed shape, so it has only one coefficient — the cubical one, \gamma.

(Writing "the linear expansion of water" is meaningless.) Its expansion is measured by watching the level in a narrow stem, and that is where the trouble starts: the vessel is expanding too, so the scale you read against is itself growing.

Apparent and real expansion

Apparent and real expansion
  • Real (absolute) expansion is the true increase in the liquid's own volume.
  • Apparent expansion is the increase measured relative to the vessel, i.e. the extra volume the liquid seems to gain as read on the vessel's own graduations.

The liquid that overflows a brim-full vessel is the apparent expansion; the real expansion is larger, because the vessel's capacity also grew and swallowed part of it.

Let the vessel be filled to the brim at the lower temperature, with volume V and coefficient \gamma_v; let the liquid's real coefficient be \gamma_r.

Vessel capacity at the higher temperature: V_v = V(1+\gamma_v\Delta T). Liquid volume at the higher temperature: V_l = V(1+\gamma_r\Delta T).

The liquid that overflows is the difference:

V_l - V_v = V(\gamma_r - \gamma_v)\Delta T

But the overflow is, by definition, the apparent expansion V\gamma_a\Delta T. Comparing the two:

\gamma_a = \gamma_r - \gamma_v \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \gamma_r = \gamma_a + \gamma_v

So the real coefficient is always larger than the apparent one, and the gap is exactly the expansion of the vessel.

For a glass vessel \gamma_v = 3\alpha_{glass} \approx 2.4\times10^{-5} K⁻¹, which is small beside mercury's 1.8\times10^{-4} but not negligible — it is about 13 % of it.

Liquid in a glass vessel \gamma_r (K⁻¹) \gamma_a = \gamma_r - \gamma_v (K⁻¹)
Mercury 1.82\times10^{-4} 1.58\times10^{-4}
Water (around 20 °C) 2.1\times10^{-4} 1.86\times10^{-4}
Alcohol 1.1\times10^{-3} 1.08\times10^{-3}
Paraffin 9.0\times10^{-4} 8.8\times10^{-4}
Worked example 9.3 — overflow from a flask

Problem. A glass flask is completely filled with 500 cm³ of a liquid at 20 °C. On heating to 70 °C, 4.0 cm³ overflows. If \gamma_v = 2.4\times10^{-5} K⁻¹, find the apparent and the real coefficients of the liquid.

Solution. \Delta T = 50 K and \gamma_a = \dfrac{\Delta V}{V\Delta T} = \dfrac{4.0}{500\times50} = 1.6\times10^{-4} K⁻¹. Then \gamma_r = \gamma_a + \gamma_v = 1.6\times10^{-4} + 0.24\times10^{-4} = 1.84\times10^{-4} K⁻¹.

The 4 cm³ that spilled understates the liquid's real growth by 0.24 × 10⁻⁴ × 500 × 50 = 0.6 cm³, which the flask absorbed by growing.

Sign and direction

\gamma_r = \gamma_a + \gamma_v, never \gamma_a - \gamma_v. If a question gives the real coefficient and asks for the overflow, subtract: the overflow is V(\gamma_r - \gamma_v)\Delta T.

Reading the relation the wrong way round is the single commonest error in this topic.

Why the level first falls, then rises

Warm a flask of coloured water gently and watch the top of the liquid in the stem. It dips slightly, then climbs steadily past its starting mark.

The reason is a race between two expansions that start at the same moment but do not have the same size. The glass in contact with the warming liquid heats up first and quickly, so the flask's capacity grows early.

The liquid as a whole is a poor conductor and warms slowly, so for the first few seconds its own expansion is still tiny. Capacity up, liquid not yet up → level down.

Once the bulk liquid warms, its much larger \gamma takes over and the level rises.

A second, quite different cause of a dip is anomalous expansion: between 0 °C and 4 °C water contracts as it warms, so its level genuinely falls.

Anomalous expansion of water

Water is not a normal liquid. From 0 °C to 4 °C it contracts; above 4 °C it expands in the ordinary way. Its density therefore peaks at 4 °C:

Consequences you can be asked to explain:

  • Ice floats, because ice (917 kg m⁻³) is less dense than water.
  • A pond freezes from the top down. The surface water cools to 4 °C and sinks; below 4 °C it is lighter and stays on top, where it freezes. The 4 °C water at the bottom lets fish survive the winter.
  • Water in a closed pipe bursts when it freezes: the 8 % expansion is resisted by the pipe, and the pressure rise is enormous.

Density falls as the temperature rises. From V = V_0(1+\gamma\Delta T) and \rho = m/V,

\rho = \frac{\rho_0}{1+\gamma\Delta T} \approx \rho_0(1-\gamma\Delta T)

so a rise of \Delta T lowers the density by the fraction \gamma\Delta T. A body's relative density falls on heating, and a solid floats a little deeper in hot water than in cold.

9.3 Heat capacity, specific heat capacity and the method of mixtures

The three quantities

Heat capacity and specific heat capacity

Heat capacity C of a body is the heat needed to raise its temperature by 1 K: C = Q/\Delta T, unit J K⁻¹. It depends on the amount of material.

Specific heat capacity c is the heat needed to raise 1 kg of the substance by 1 K: c = \dfrac{Q}{m\Delta T}, unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. It is a property of the material only.

Molar heat capacity is the heat needed to raise 1 mol by 1 K, unit J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

So Q = mc\Delta T = C\Delta T, and C = mc. A 2 kg block of copper has twice the heat capacity of a 1 kg block, but the same specific heat capacity.

Substance c (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) Substance c (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Water 4200 Brass 380
Ice 2100 Copper 390
Steam 2010 Iron, steel 480
Kerosene 2100 Aluminium 900
Mercury 140 Lead 130

Water's specific heat is unusually large — about ten times that of copper.

That one number explains why water is used as a coolant in vehicle radiators, why a hot-water bottle stays warm for hours, why coastal climates are milder than inland ones, and why a kettle of water takes so long to boil.

It is also why water is the standard calorimetric liquid: a given mass of water changes temperature slowly, so a mixture experiment is easy to time.

Water equivalent

A calorimeter is a metal cup, and it takes heat too. Rather than carry its mass and specific heat through every calculation, we convert it into the mass of water that would take the same heat for the same temperature rise:

W = \frac{m_c c_c}{c_w} \quad\text{(in kg)} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \text{heat capacity of calorimeter} = Wc_w

A copper calorimeter of mass 0.10 kg and c = 390 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ has water equivalent W = 0.10\times390/4200 = 0.0093 kg = 9.3 g. Its heat capacity is 9.3\times10^{-3}\times4200 = 39 J K⁻¹.

The method of mixtures

Principle of calorimetry

In an isolated system, heat lost by the hot bodies = heat gained by the cold bodies. No heat is created or destroyed; it only moves.

Put a hot solid of mass m_1, specific heat c_1, at temperature \theta_1 into water of mass m_2 at \theta_2, inside a calorimeter of water equivalent W. If the final temperature is \theta (with \theta_2 < \theta < \theta_1):

m_1c_1(\theta_1-\theta) = (m_2c_w + Wc_w)(\theta-\theta_2)

Every bracket is positive: a hot body falls from \theta_1 to \theta, so its change is \theta_1-\theta; a cold body rises from \theta_2 to \theta, so its change is \theta-\theta_2.

Writing the two brackets the same way round is the source of most sign errors in this topic.

Worked example 9.4 — finding a specific heat

Problem. A 0.10 kg block of metal at 100 °C is dropped into 0.20 kg of water at 20 °C in a calorimeter of water equivalent 0.02 kg. The final temperature is 25 °C. Find the specific heat of the metal. (c_w = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.)

Solution. Heat gained by the water and calorimeter: (0.20 + 0.02)\times4200\times(25-20) = 0.22\times4200\times5 = 4620 J. Heat lost by the metal: 0.10\times c\times(100-25) = 7.5c. Equating: 7.5c = 4620, so c = 616 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ ≈ 6.2\times10^2 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

If the calorimeter had been ignored, the heat gained would have been taken as 0.20\times4200\times5 = 4200 J and the answer would have come out as 560 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ — 9 % too low. That is the size of the error a 20 g water equivalent makes.

Three ways a mixture answer goes wrong
  1. Ignoring the calorimeter. Its water equivalent must be added to the water mass. Leaving it out always makes the hot body's specific heat come out too low (too little heat is credited to the cold side).
  2. Sign flip. Use (\theta_1-\theta) for the hot side and (\theta-\theta_2) for the cold side. A negative answer means you reversed one of them.
  3. Stopping at 0 °C. If ice is involved, check first whether all the ice can melt with the heat available. If it cannot, the final temperature is 0 °C with some ice left, and the water term must not be used at all.

Newton's law of cooling

Newton's law of cooling

The rate at which a body loses heat to its surroundings is directly proportional to the excess of its temperature over the surroundings, provided that excess is small and the surroundings are at a constant temperature:

\frac{dQ}{dt} = k(\theta-\theta_s)

Since dQ = -mc\,d\theta for the body, the same law can be written as a statement about the rate of fall of temperature:

\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -K(\theta-\theta_s), \qquad K = \frac{k}{mc}

Integrating from \theta_0 at t = 0:

\theta - \theta_s = (\theta_0-\theta_s)\,e^{-Kt}

so the excess temperature decays exponentially. Three consequences the paper uses:

  • The hotter body cools faster. At 90 °C in a 25 °C room the body loses heat five times as fast as at 38 °C. This is why a cup of tea is drinkable in ten minutes but takes an hour to come down to room temperature.
  • A plot of \ln(\theta-\theta_s) against t is a straight line of slope -K. That is the standard experimental verification of the law.
  • The law is only a small-excess approximation to Stefan's law. For a body much hotter than its surroundings, radiation loss grows as T^4 and Newton's law fails.
Worked example 9.5 — cooling coffee in Kathmandu

Problem. A cup of coffee at 90 °C is left in a room at 25 °C. It cools to 70 °C in 5 minutes. How long will it take to reach 50 °C?

Solution. Excess temperatures: initially 90-25 = 65 K, after 5 min 70-25 = 45 K. From the exponential law, 45 = 65e^{-5K}, so K = \frac{1}{5}\ln(65/45) = 0.0734 min⁻¹.

For 50 °C the excess is 25 K: 25 = 65e^{-Kt}, so t = \frac{\ln(65/25)}{0.0734} = \frac{0.9555}{0.0734} = 13 min.

The first 20 K took 5 min; the next 20 K takes 8 min — the cooling slows as the excess shrinks. Any answer that gives equal times for equal temperature drops has used a linear law by mistake.

Cooling correction. In a real mixture experiment the calorimeter loses heat to the room while the mixture settles.

Newton's law supplies the fix: plot the temperature against time, and extrapolate the cooling curve backwards to the instant of mixing.

The corrected final temperature is slightly higher than the highest reading, and the corrected initial rate is read from the same graph.

This is why the experiment is stirred quickly, started close to room temperature, and finished fast.

9.4 Latent heat of fusion and vaporization; the triple point

Latent heat

While ice melts at 0 °C, its temperature does not rise, however hard you heat it. The heat is doing something else: it is pulling the molecules out of the rigid lattice and into the liquid.

The energy goes into potential energy of the molecules, not into their kinetic energy — and temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy. Only when the last crystal has melted does the thermometer start to climb again.

Specific latent heat

The specific latent heat L of a substance is the heat needed to change 1 kg of it from one phase to another at constant temperature:

Q = mL \qquad L = \frac{Q}{m}\ \text{(J kg}^{-1}\text{)}

  • Latent heat of fusion L_f: solid → liquid (melting), or liquid → solid (freezing, same value released).
  • Latent heat of vaporization L_v: liquid → vapour (boiling or evaporating), or vapour → liquid (condensing, same value released).
Change Substance Specific latent heat
Fusion (melting) Ice at 0 °C 3.36\times10^5 J kg⁻¹ (80 cal g⁻¹)
Vaporization Water at 100 °C 2.26\times10^6 J kg⁻¹ (540 cal g⁻¹)
Sublimation Ice → vapour at 0 °C 2.83\times10^6 J kg⁻¹

Note how large L_v is: boiling 1 g of water takes about 5.4 times as much heat as heating it from 0 °C to 100 °C.

That is why steam is such an effective heating medium, and why a burn from steam is far worse than a burn from boiling water: the steam first gives up 2260 J g⁻¹ of latent heat as it condenses on the skin, and only then does the resulting 100 °C water cool.

Evaporation versus boiling. Evaporation happens at any temperature, from the surface only, and cools the remaining liquid (the fastest molecules leave).

Boiling happens at one fixed temperature for a given pressure, throughout the liquid, when the saturated vapour pressure equals the external pressure.

That is why water boils at about 95 °C in Kathmandu (air pressure ≈ 0.88 atm) and at 71 °C on the summit of Sagarmatha — and why a pressure cooker, by raising the pressure, raises the boiling point and cooks dal faster.

The heating curve

The curve is the whole of calorimetry in one picture. To find the heat to take a mass m from one point to another, add up the straight sloped pieces (mc\Delta T) and the flat pieces (mL) that lie between them.

Doing the phase bookkeeping

An ice problem is not one equation but a decision tree. Work in this order and never skip step 2:

  1. Heat available. How much heat would the warm bodies release if they cooled to 0 °C? (Include the calorimeter.)
  2. Heat needed to melt all the ice. Q = mL_f. Compare it with step 1. - If step 1 < step 2, the final temperature is 0 °C and some ice survives. The answer is "0 °C, with m_{left} = m - Q_1/L_f of ice remaining". - If step 1 > step 2, all the ice melts; go on.
  3. Leftover heat. Subtract the melting heat from the available heat. Use the remainder to warm the whole final mass — original water plus calorimeter plus melted ice — and solve for \Delta T.
Worked example 9.6 — ice into water, with the calorimeter

Problem. 20 g of ice at 0 °C is dropped into 180 g of water at 30 °C in a calorimeter of water equivalent 20 g. Find the final temperature. (c_w = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_f = 3.36\times10^5 J kg⁻¹.)

Solution. Step 1 — heat available if everything cools to 0 °C. The water plus the calorimeter behave as 200 g of water: Q_1 = 0.200\times4200\times30 = 25\,200 J.

Step 2 — heat to melt all the ice. Q_2 = 0.020\times3.36\times10^5 = 6720 J. Since 6720 < 25\,200, all the ice melts and the mixture ends above 0 °C.

Step 3 — warm the final mixture. Leftover heat = 25\,200 - 6720 = 18\,480 J. The final mass that must be warmed is 180 + 20 + 20 = 220 g (original water, calorimeter equivalent, melted ice), so \Delta T = \dfrac{18\,480}{0.220\times4200} = \dfrac{18\,480}{924} = 20 K.

Answer. The final temperature is 20 °C.

Check the balance the other way: the water cools 30 → 20 °C, releasing 0.200\times4200\times10 = 8400 J; the ice absorbs 6720 J to melt and 0.020\times4200\times20 = 1680 J to warm to 20 °C, total 8400 J. It balances.

Worked example 9.7 — ice at −10 °C to steam at 100 °C

Problem. How much heat is needed to convert 10 g of ice at −10 °C into steam at 100 °C? (c_{ice} = 2100, c_w = 4200, L_f = 3.36\times10^5, L_v = 2.26\times10^6, all SI.)

Solution. Four separate stages, in order:

Stage Process Heat (J)
1 warm the ice −10 → 0 °C 0.010\times2100\times10 = 210
2 melt the ice at 0 °C 0.010\times3.36\times10^5 = 3360
3 warm the water 0 → 100 °C 0.010\times4200\times100 = 4200
4 boil the water at 100 °C 0.010\times2.26\times10^6 = 22\,600
total 30 370 J ≈ 3.04 × 10⁴ J

Stage 4 alone is three-quarters of the total. The heat is not one mc\Delta T: each stage uses its own specific heat or its own latent heat, and the total is a sum of four numbers.

"Steam at 100 °C" is not "water at 100 °C"

A gram of steam at 100 °C contains 2260 J more than a gram of water at 100 °C. Every statement about "which is hotter" must be about temperature; every statement about "which contains more heat" must count the latent heat.

The two are different questions, and the paper asks both.

The triple point

Triple point

The triple point of a substance is the unique temperature and pressure at which its solid, liquid and vapour phases coexist in equilibrium. For water it is

T_3 = 273.16\ \text{K} = 0.01\ ^\circ\text{C}, \qquad P_3 = 611\ \text{Pa} \approx 4.58\ \text{mm of mercury}

At any other pressure only two phases can be in equilibrium at a given temperature (ice and water at 0 °C and 1 atm, for example).

Why the paper cares about it:

  • It is a single, reproducible fixed point — one temperature and one pressure — so it is far better as a thermometer calibration than the melting point, which depends on pressure. The kelvin was defined from the triple point of water from 1954 until the 2019 redefinition of the SI.
  • Melting point ≠ triple point. Ice melts at 273.15 K (0.00 °C) under 1 atm, but at 273.16 K under 611 Pa. The two differ by 0.01 K because the melting point depends on pressure.
  • The triple point pressure is below atmospheric, so ice does not sublime at 1 atm; it melts. Sublimation of ice is common in the dry, thin air of the high Himalayas, where the vapour pressure is very low.

The same idea applies to carbon dioxide, whose triple point is at 5.1 atm — above atmospheric pressure. That is why "dry ice" does not melt at room pressure: it sublimes straight to gas.

Formula and fact sheet

Topic Formula or fact
Linear expansion \Delta L = L\alpha\Delta T; L' = L(1+\alpha\Delta T)
Area, volume \Delta A = A\beta\Delta T, \Delta V = V\gamma\Delta T
The relation \beta = 2\alpha, \gamma = 3\alpha (isotropic solid, \alpha\Delta T\ll1)
Units all three in K⁻¹; α (solids) ~10⁻⁵, γ (liquids) ~10⁻⁴, γ (gases) ~10⁻³
Hole in a plate grows on heating, exactly as a disc of the same material would
Bimetallic strip bends with the larger-α metal on the outside when heated; towards the smaller-α metal
Thermal stress \sigma = Y\alpha\Delta T (compressive on heating), F = YA\alpha\Delta T
Pendulum clock \dfrac{\Delta T_p}{T_p} = \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta\theta; loses time when hot
Time lost per day \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta\theta\times86400 s
Real vs apparent \gamma_r = \gamma_a + \gamma_v, with \gamma_v = 3\alpha_{vessel}
Overflow \Delta V = V(\gamma_r - \gamma_v)\Delta T
Density on heating \rho = \rho_0(1+\gamma\Delta T)^{-1}\approx\rho_0(1-\gamma\Delta T)
Water anomaly maximum density 1000 kg m⁻³ at 4 °C; ice 917 kg m⁻³
Heat capacity C = Q/\Delta T (J K⁻¹); C = mc
Specific heat Q = mc\Delta T (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Water equivalent W = m_cc_c/c_w; heat capacity of calorimeter = Wc_w
Method of mixtures m_1c_1(\theta_1-\theta) = (m_2c_w + Wc_w)(\theta-\theta_2)
Latent heat Q = mL (J kg⁻¹); L_f = 3.36\times10^5, L_v = 2.26\times10^6 J kg⁻¹
Sublimation L_{sub}\approx L_f + L_v (with L_v at 0 °C) = 2.83\times10^6 J kg⁻¹
Newton's cooling \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = k(\theta-\theta_s); \theta-\theta_s = (\theta_0-\theta_s)e^{-Kt}
Cooling check \ln(\theta-\theta_s) vs t is a straight line of slope -K
Triple point of water 273.16 K (0.01 °C), 611 Pa (4.58 mm Hg); all three phases coexist
Useful constants 1 cal = 4.2 J; c_w = 4200, c_{ice} = 2100, c_{steam} = 2010 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹

Chapter summary

  • \Delta L = L\alpha\Delta T, \Delta A = A\beta\Delta T, \Delta V = V\gamma\Delta T, with \beta = 2\alpha and \gamma = 3\alpha for an isotropic solid. Area takes 2\alpha, volume takes 3\alpha — never the other way round.
  • A hole or a cavity in a heated plate grows by the same fraction as the metal itself; nothing shrinks on heating except water below 4 °C.
  • A clamped rod develops \sigma = Y\alpha\Delta T, compressive on heating. A pendulum clock runs slow when hot, losing \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta\theta of its time.
  • A liquid's real expansion exceeds its apparent expansion by the vessel's: \gamma_r = \gamma_a + \gamma_v. The level in a warmed vessel first dips (the glass grows first) and then rises.
  • Water is densest at 4 °C; that is why ice floats, ponds freeze from the top, and pipes burst in a hard frost.
  • Q = mc\Delta T raises temperature; Q = mL changes phase at constant temperature. Never use both for the same stage.
  • The calorimeter's water equivalent W = m_cc_c/c_w must be added to the water mass. Ignoring it makes the hot body's specific heat come out too low.
  • In an ice problem, first compare the heat available with mL_f. If the ice cannot all melt, the final temperature is 0 °C with ice left over.
  • Newton's law of cooling gives exponential cooling; equal temperature drops take longer and longer, and the hotter body cools faster.
  • The triple point of water is 273.16 K at 611 Pa — the one state where ice, water and vapour coexist, and the reason the melting point (273.15 K at 1 atm) is not the same number.

1. (c) — length is one dimension, area two, volume three, so the coefficients go as 1 : 2 : 3. Option (b) is the area coefficient.

2. (d) — α is a fractional change of length per kelvin, so the metre cancels and K⁻¹ is left.

3. (b) — every linear dimension of the plate grows by the fraction αΔT, and the hole is one of them. A hole behaves like a disc of the same metal.

4. (a) — brass lengthens more, so it must form the longer (outer) arc. The strip curves towards the metal with the smaller α.

5. (d) — between 0 °C and 4 °C water contracts, and above 4 °C it expands; the turning point is the density maximum.

6. (c) — heat per unit mass per kelvin: J/(kg K).

7. (a) — the water equivalent is a mass of water whose heat capacity equals the calorimeter's. Option (c) is the heat capacity itself, in J K⁻¹.

8. (b) — 80 cal g⁻¹ × 4.2 = 336 J g⁻¹ = 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. The 10⁶ value in (a) is the latent heat of vaporization.

11. (c) — that is the definition: solid, liquid and vapour in equilibrium at one temperature and pressure.

12. (a) — the vessel's growth hides part of the liquid's growth, so the real coefficient is the larger one.

13. (c) — gases have γ ≈ 3.7 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, some twenty times a liquid's and a few hundred times a solid's.

14. (d) — the driving difference is the body's temperature minus the surroundings'. Option (b) is Stefan's law, which Newton's law approximates for small excess.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (b) — a longer pendulum has a longer period T = 2π√(L/g), so each swing takes more time and the clock falls behind. g does not change measurably with the weather.

2. (d) — ΔL = LαΔT with L and ΔT the same, so ΔL ∝ α: the ratio is 1 : 2.

3. (a) — ΔL/L = αΔT, ΔA/A = 2αΔT, ΔV/V = 3αΔT, so the fractional changes are in the ratio of the dimensions, 1 : 2 : 3.

4. (b) — on cooling, brass contracts more than iron, so brass becomes the shorter (inner) surface. The bend reverses direction.

5. (a) — γₐ = γᵣ − γᵥ = 0 means γᵣ = γᵥ. The liquid does expand; the vessel expands by exactly as much, so nothing seems to change.

6. (c) — melting takes 336 J g⁻¹ of latent heat from the drink before the ice water can warm at all. The temperature of both is 0 °C, so (a) is wrong.

7. (c) — condensing steam gives up 2260 J g⁻¹ before the 100 °C water even starts to cool. Both are at the same temperature.

8. (b) — the heat actually gained by the cold side is larger than m_w c_w Δθ; ignoring W makes the numerator too small, so c comes out too low.

9. (b) — ρ = m/V, so a fractional rise γΔT in volume gives the same fractional fall in density.

10. (a) — the rate is proportional to the excess temperature, which is largest at the start. That is why the cooling curve is steepest at the beginning.

11. (a) — invar's α is about 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹, ten times smaller than steel's, so the length hardly changes and the clock keeps time in all weathers.

12. (d) — volumes go as the cube of the radius, 1 : 8, and ΔV = VγΔT with the same γ and ΔT.

13. (c) — water contracts from 0 °C to 4 °C (the anomalous region) and expands above 4 °C, so the volume is least at 4 °C.

14. (d) — the heat breaks the bonds of the lattice, increasing the molecules' potential energy. The average kinetic energy, and therefore the temperature, stays the same.

15. (b) — Δθ = Q/(mc), so with Q and m equal, Δθ ∝ 1/c: kerosene's c is half of water's, so its rise is twice as large.

Model answer D1: thermal expansion of solids and liquids (10 marks)

Introduction. Most substances expand on heating because the molecules vibrate with greater amplitude and the average distance between them increases.

Coefficients. The coefficient of linear expansion is \alpha = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L\,\Delta\theta}, of area expansion \beta = \dfrac{\Delta A}{A\,\Delta\theta}, and of volume expansion \gamma = \dfrac{\Delta V}{V\,\Delta\theta}.

The unit of each is K⁻¹ (or ^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}).

Relation. For a square plate of side L, the new side is L(1 + \alpha\theta), so the new area is L^2(1 + \alpha\theta)^2 \approx L^2(1 + 2\alpha\theta) and \beta = 2\alpha.

For a cube the volume is L^3(1 + 3\alpha\theta) and \gamma = 3\alpha. Hence \alpha:\beta:\gamma = 1:2:3.

Liquids. A liquid has two coefficients. The apparent expansion is what we see relative to the vessel, and the real expansion adds the expansion of the vessel: \gamma_r = \gamma_a + \gamma_g. The density changes as \rho' = \rho/(1 + \gamma\theta).

Anomalous expansion of water. Between 0^{\circ}\text{C} and 4^{\circ}\text{C} water contracts when heated, so its density is maximum, 1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}, at 4^{\circ}\text{C}. Above 4^{\circ}\text{C} it expands normally.

In a lake in winter, the surface cools to 4^{\circ}\text{C} and sinks; then the surface water cools further and freezes first. Ice floats and insulates the water below, so fish survive.

Material \alpha\ (\text{K}^{-1})
Steel 1.2\times10^{-5}
Aluminium 2.3\times10^{-5}
Glass (ordinary) 0.9\times10^{-5}
Invar \approx 10^{-6}

Applications and effects. Gaps in railway tracks and bridges, rivetting hot, fitting an iron tyre on a wheel, the bimetal thermostat and the compensated pendulum of a clock (invar), all use expansion.

Numerical. A steel rail 30\ \text{m} long at 20^{\circ}\text{C} is heated to 50^{\circ}\text{C}: \Delta L = 30\times1.2\times10^{-5}\times30 = 1.08\times10^{-2}\ \text{m} = 10.8\ \text{mm}.

If it could not expand, the thermal stress would be Y\alpha\Delta\theta = 2\times10^{11}\times1.2\times10^{-5}\times30 = 7.2\times10^{7}\ \text{Pa}.

Conclusion. \gamma = 3\alpha for isotropic solids, and water's maximum density at 4^{\circ}\text{C} protects aquatic life.

Model answer D2: calorimetry, specific heat and latent heat (10 marks)

Introduction. Heat is the energy that flows because of a temperature difference. Its SI unit is joule (1\ \text{cal} = 4.2\ \text{J}).

Definitions.

  1. Heat capacity C = Q/\Delta\theta (J K⁻¹).
  2. Specific heat capacity c = \dfrac{Q}{m\,\Delta\theta} (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). For water c = 4200, which is high, so water is a good coolant and the sea moderates the climate.
  3. Latent heat L = Q/m is the heat to change the state at constant temperature. For ice, L_f = 3.36\times10^5\ \text{J kg}^{-1} and for steam, L_v = 2.26\times10^6\ \text{J kg}^{-1}.

Principle of calorimetry. If no heat is lost, the heat lost by the hot bodies equals the heat gained by the cold bodies. This follows from the conservation of energy.

Process Heat formula
Temperature change Q = mc\,\Delta\theta
Melting or freezing Q = mL_f
Boiling or condensing Q = mL_v
Water equivalent W = mc/c_{water}

Numerical. 50\ \text{g} of ice at 0^{\circ}\text{C} is added to 200\ \text{g} of water at 40^{\circ}\text{C} in an insulated vessel. Heat needed to melt the ice = 0.050\times3.36\times10^5 = 16\,800\ \text{J}.

Heat the water can give up in cooling to 0^{\circ}\text{C} = 0.200\times4200\times40 = 33\,600\ \text{J}, which is more, so all the ice melts.

The remaining 16\,800\ \text{J} warms the total 250\ \text{g}: \Delta\theta = \dfrac{16\,800}{0.250\times4200} = 16^{\circ}\text{C}. The final temperature is 16^{\circ}\text{C}.

Conclusion. Calorimetry rests on energy conservation. During a change of state the temperature stays constant, because the heat is used to break molecular bonds.
